title: Escalate a ten minute challenge in clear phases
text: For a roughly 10 minute challenge, escalate in three readable phases: baseline from 0:00 to 3:30, about 30% stronger from 3:31 to 7:00, and about 50% stronger from 7:01 to 10:00. Existing units keep the stats they had when summoned, so later upgrades do not retroactively change them, and their level stays visible. The transferable lesson is to make escalation predictable and legible, whether through battle chapters or a runner route that becomes denser with hazards.
use_when: Pacing a long session that needs a rising arc without surprising players with hidden stat changes.
do: Escalate in readable phases rather than continuously
Give each phase a clear milestone and stronger finale
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Make the climax require coordinated preparation
text: Make a spectacular finale something players earn through coordinated movement, not a single button press. In the source, an 80 mana Meteor Shower creates impact zones that a Vanguard must run over to lock the target before a wide area strike and visual transformation. Adapt the reasoning within the engine as a final sequence of ordered checkpoints before the portal, so preparation creates anticipation and the finish feels collectively earned.
use_when: Designing a memorable team finale or final objective that should involve bodies and communication.
do: Require several players or steps to prepare a climax
Place the decisive action in the play space before the payoff
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Balance powerful effects with cost and counterplay
text: Pair powerful tactical effects with meaningful cost, limits, and a chance for opponents to respond. The source prices area turrets at 40 mana, an invisible stunning mine at 20 mana with a 5 second cooldown, and temporary 15 second power boosts at 50 to 60 mana. Hidden area damage plus stun can feel unfair, so in this engine prefer the visible red hazard circles and reserve dramatic moments for clearly signposted checkpoints or the portal finish.
use_when: A creator asks for traps, stuns, or other high impact abilities that could remove player agency.
do: Show dangerous zones before players commit
Reserve strong effects for costly, limited moments
avoid: Invisible unavoidable punishment
Long or frequent surprise stuns
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Use a limited comeback window, not a permanent catch-up buff
text: Trigger a comeback state only when a team is in clear crisis, such as holding under 20% of the field, and end it after recovery above 25%. A strong but bounded example doubles resource regeneration from 5 to 10 per second and permits only 2 activations, giving the losing side one counterattack opportunity without erasing the leader's advantage. Make the state and its remaining uses legible so players know they must plan the counterattack rather than rely on rescue.
use_when: A competitive design needs comeback potential without making an early lead meaningless.
do: Set separate entry and exit thresholds.
Cap the number of comeback activations.
Show when the comeback state ends.
avoid: Leaving the losing team's buff active indefinitely.
Making recovery automatic without player planning.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Build accessibility by removing systems, not only shortening rounds
text: For a fast casual mode, use a fixed 5-minute round with the winner decided only when time expires. Remove carrying, decks, mana management and armor exceptions, then give each role one immediate verb and cooldown-only skills; a frequently usable support action can have a 10-second cooldown. Add automatic pressure at a steady interval, such as every 10 seconds, so play continues even when participants do not coordinate.
use_when: A standard game has too many rules for first-time or mixed-skill players.
do: Use one clear objective per role.
Replace resource economies with visible cooldowns.
Keep the round ending predictable.
avoid: Keeping every subsystem and merely increasing game speed.
Making success depend on a specialist role being present.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Redirect territory-shooter requests to supported contests
text: Do not promise painting territory, guns, instant kills, unit summons or team territory control, because none of these engines supports them. For competition, offer an online runner race on separate copies with a live leaderboard, ordered checkpoints worth 100 each and a finish worth 300 plus a time bonus. For direct action, offer battle chapters using sword combos, dodging and a boss, and treat territory or faction war as theme and story rather than a simulated mechanic.
use_when: The creator asks for a paint war, shooting match, commander units or territorial conquest.
do: Name the unsupported mechanic kindly.
Offer racing for competition or sword battles for action.
Preserve the desired fiction through labels and scenery.
avoid: Promising team painting or shooting.
Describing cosmetic territory theming as actual control mechanics.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Let one moving frontline carry the contest
text: For a tug-of-war contest, have opposing forces seek the nearest rival and stop where they meet, so the clash itself draws a clear border instead of making players read several meters. Reward victories by advancing that border, and maintain free baseline pressure: the source releases 3 soldiers every 15 seconds without Mana. When adapting this to another engine, preserve the single readable struggle and steady rhythm rather than copying unsupported minions.
use_when: Designing a territorial or back-and-forth contest that spectators and players must read instantly.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Use a slow, contested boss to break stalemates
text: Reserve a boss for the middle or late game, and gate it behind visible preparation: a full charge, delivery to a marked summon point, then a Commander resource and skill check. Make the resulting threat slow, highly visible and hard to interrupt so the opposing team has time to respond; in the source, reaching the back line repaints 90% of the field, but killing the boss awards substantial territory instead. The design lesson is a dramatic finale with counterplay and a meaningful reversal, not an automatic win button.
use_when: A match can stall and needs a coordinated climax that both teams can contest.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Make teamwork a short cross-role power window
text: Express synergy as an explicit sequence in which one role creates an opening and another exploits a temporary empowerment, rather than as a passive bonus. The source uses a 10-second window for an enlarged Vanguard to paint trails again and a 15-second window for a Striker's shots to paint the floor directly. Clearly signal activation and expiry, and give the pair an immediate shared target so the short window produces a memorable coordinated push.
use_when: Designing cooperative roles and wanting teamwork to produce visible, timed highlights.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Redirect shooter and territory-control wishes by their desired experience
text: A request for a VR team shooter or territory-control battle often includes rifles, revives, mana cards and floor painting, none of which this engine supports. Say that plainly, then preserve the underlying wish: battle provides sword action, dodging and staged enemies; tactics provides spatial control through ordered captures and guarded squares; an online runner race provides group competition with a live leaderboard. When presenting three options, use these as three genuinely different genres rather than three versions of the unavailable shooter.
use_when: A creator asks for 3v3 combat, gun roles, territory painting, revives or card-triggered team powers.
do: Name the unsupported mechanics before proposing alternatives.
Offer battle for direct action, tactics for spatial control, and an online runner race for group competition.
avoid: Promising rifles, mana cards, minion revives, floor painting, or role-specific abilities.
Presenting three options that are merely variations of one unsupported team-combat brief.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Build combat beats around a visible opening and a quick payoff
text: A setup-and-payoff beat makes action feel cooperative and intentional: one event creates a clearly marked opening, and a quick physical response converts it into a strong result. The source uses a flashing floor marker lasting 2 to 3 seconds, a useful starting window to playtest for notice-and-respond actions. In this engine, recreate the rhythm within supported battle play through warning rings, a short dodge or reposition, then a sword response, rather than adding stuns or role abilities.
use_when: A battle encounter feels like undifferentiated attacking and needs clearer pacing, readability and satisfying decisions.
do: Make the opportunity visible with a floor marker or warning ring.
Playtest whether a new player can notice, move and respond within the window.
Leave a recovery beat before introducing the next threat.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Make cooperation a visible two-step handoff
text: Build team combos so one role creates an opportunity and another completes it, rather than asking everyone to act at once. Here, damage adds a Stun Marker and a floor light tells the Vanguard where to step, while another combo grants 15 seconds of enhanced attacks. Use a conspicuous world-space cue, a clear completion action, and an immediate result so teammates can coordinate without a tutorial.
use_when: Designing cooperative roles, team abilities, or moments that should make spectators understand who helped whom
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Let planning resources recover during deliberation
text: A strategic player should not become helpless while thinking: this economy generates 5 Mana per second up to a 100 cap, reaching full from empty in 20 seconds. Discarding an unwanted card refunds 15 Mana, giving players an emergency conversion from bad options into tempo. Pair steady regeneration with a capped reserve and a costly refund so recovery is possible but still requires a decision.
use_when: Tuning a resource-driven role and checking that players always have a path back into play
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Guarantee a basic action inside a varied hand
text: Keep one inexpensive, dependable card permanently available, redraw it after use with only a 1-second cooldown, and add variety through nine rotation cards drawn four at a time. The example basic unit costs 5 Mana, only one second of passive income, so a bad random hand cannot remove the player's ability to participate. This structure separates reliability from variety and makes each draw easier to read.
use_when: Designing randomized hands, decks, or rotating action choices that must never leave a player stuck
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Express unit jobs through a readable cost ladder
text: Give each unit a distinct tactical job and make its cost communicate commitment: 5 Mana for disposable lane filler, 10 for a fast raider, 20 for a self-destruct attacker, and 30 for a large territory-capturing unit. At 5 Mana per second, those costs imply roughly 1, 2, 4, and 6 seconds of saving, creating an understandable tempo ladder. Also distinguish battlefield consequences, such as whether a destroyed unit paints the floor, so players can predict the strategic effect before spending.
use_when: Balancing several unit or action types whose purpose and opportunity cost should be quickly understood
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Build a five minute battle toward a boss climax
text: For a short action session, use a three-part arc: minutes 0:00 to 2:00 establish the core fight with simple enemies, minutes 2:00 to 4:00 raise pressure and introduce the boss confrontation, and minutes 4:00 to 5:00 become a decisive final rush. Give the ending a clear resolution rather than letting intensity simply stop. In this engine, express the arc through successive battle chapters, enemy mixes such as grunts, shields and beasts, then the boss, with rain reserved for added late pressure.
use_when: Structuring pacing and difficulty for a short battle game or chapter sequence.
do: Teach the core enemy response before adding mixed pressure.
Place the boss after the opening learning phase.
Make the last minute feel decisive and end clearly.
avoid: Starting with the boss before players learn the fight.
Keeping intensity flat across the whole session.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Redirect hero-skill territory control wishes
text: Requests for summoned minions, turret drops, meteor attacks, boss armies, shooting weak points, or painting territory cannot be built by these engines, even when they fit a MOBA fantasy. Offer battle for close action with a sword, dash, telegraphed danger rings, chapters and a boss, or tactics for territorial-feeling play through ordered captures, guard patterns and route planning on a 6 x 8 board. In MR, preserve real walking and safety rather than simulating a battlefield with running players.
use_when: A creator asks for MOBA hero abilities, team territory control, shooting, or summoned armies.
do: Name the unsupported mechanics kindly before proposing an alternative.
Choose battle for direct action or tactics for spatial conquest.
Keep MR encounters walkable with clearly telegraphed hazards.
avoid: Promising turrets, meteors, shooting, armies, or floor-painting systems.
Treating a theme or story as permission to add new mechanics.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Open with a short, spectacular movement burst
text: For a timed area-control game, make the first 3 seconds unusually generous: every crossed row changes colour, creating instant visible progress before normal play begins. A midpoint race can add a capped bonus of 1 to 3 extra rows, scaled by the arrival-time gap, but this rewards an early lead and can snowball. Keep the opening easy to understand and treat the bonus as a dramatic kickoff, not the deciding mechanic.
use_when: Designing the opening and scoring rhythm of a competitive movement game
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Make specialist roles depend on one another
text: A 3v3, 10-minute match can divide expertise across physical area control and blocking, precision ranged play, and planning or unit management. The important pattern is interdependence, not three separate minigames: the commander can only deploy the ultimate boss after the vanguard physically places a summon box. Give the team's biggest moment a visible handoff between roles so every specialist contributes to it.
use_when: A creator wants distinct team roles and cooperative highlight moments
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Translate territory-control wishes into supported competition
text: If a creator asks for 3v3 territory control, ranged shooting, deployable turrets, or summonable units, explain that these mechanics are not available rather than reskinning them as promises. Preserve the underlying wish with a choice: timed tactics boards for planning and ordered captures, battle chapters for direct physical action, or an online runner race with a live leaderboard for group competition. Ask whether strategy, combat fantasy, or head-to-head rivalry matters most before choosing.
use_when: A creator brings a team shooter or territory-control brief to this engine
do: Offer tactics for strategy, battle for action, or an online runner race for rivalry.
Identify the desired experience before selecting the closest genre.
avoid: Do not promise teams capturing floor colour, shooting, turrets, or boss summoning.
Do not describe an online race as shared territorial combat.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Make the boss a costly gamble, not a free power spike
text: Gate a climax behind a substantial resource cost, such as the source's 90 mana, and make a failed skill check consume the attempt rather than merely delay a button press. Give the boss very high durability and very slow movement so its threat is readable, then balance its huge upside with a severe, visible penalty if it dies and make a second summon unlikely. In this engine, keep only the pacing lesson: build a chapter-end boss as a slow, readable, high-stakes finale, without promising mana, summoning, territory painting or stun systems.
use_when: Designing a boss finale or a comeback moment with major risk and reward
do: Telegraph the slow approach so players have time to react
Make both the potential reward and the defeat penalty clear before commitment
avoid: A free boss that only adds power
An instantly repeatable summon after failure
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Converge a climactic clash on one shared objective
text: When two major threats meet, turning their collision into a distinct duel phase concentrates attention instead of splitting it across the whole field. Give everyone the same immediate objective, focus the opposing threat, and use a bounded winner reward such as the source's 20% health recovery while the loser suffers the established defeat penalty. For FortalLand, reuse only the focus and phase-change lesson in a solo boss chapter: briefly change existing boss behavior and give the player one obvious priority using sword hits, dashes, warning rings and available enemies.
use_when: A boss encounter has several threats and the player may not know what matters now
do: Announce the phase change through a clear behavior shift
Keep one dominant objective during the climax
avoid: Competing objectives with equal visual urgency
Promoting a two-boss or unit-control system the engine lacks
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Turn defense into readable vulnerabilities, not invisible math
text: Defense becomes actionable when play can change it: the source uses repeated weak-point critical hits to break armor, after which every friendly damage source benefits, and distinguishes ordinary units from structures. Keep defense classes few and visibly different, and clearly explain any zero-damage result when attack is equal to or below armor. In this engine, express the lesson through existing behaviors, such as a shield blocking frontal hits and a beast telegraphing its charge, rather than adding armor statistics, critical hits, plasma weapons or structures.
use_when: Designing battle enemies whose defense should change how the player approaches them
do: Give each defensive behavior a visible cue and a counter
Show when a successful hit changes the enemy's vulnerability
avoid: Unexplained immunity or zero damage
A hidden stack of armor classes and weapon exceptions
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

title: Translate MOBA territory skills into supported objectives
text: A request for painting team territory, summoning a 5 x 5 cannon turret on a 20-second cooldown, or clearing a 10 x 10 area with a meteor on a 30-second cooldown cannot be built directly. Preserve the intended push-and-defend tension with battle chapters containing grunts, shields and beasts, ending in a boss, or with tactics boards that require ordered target captures while avoiding guards. For a contest over progress rather than combat, use a runner race with ordered checkpoints and a live leaderboard.
use_when: A creator describes MOBA-style territory control, deployable turrets, or large cooldown-based attacks.
do: Ask whether the desired feeling is defending against waves, outcapturing rivals, or escaping danger.
Offer battle chapters and a boss for the wave-defense fantasy.
Offer ordered tactics captures or a checkpoint race for territorial progress.
avoid: Promising team-color painting, turret placement, meteor attacks, or cooldown skills.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground casual mode GDD, example 2 (course material)

title: Telegraph floor hazards before resolving them
text: For a grid-based survival challenge, flash threatened tiles orange for 3 seconds, then turn lava tiles red and safe tiles green so players can read the state at a glance. In the PC proof of concept, a 10 x 20 grid, a circle for the player, WASD movement and 5 HP were enough to test the loop. Awarding 10 points for avoiding lava and subtracting 10 for being hit makes every round immediately legible; tune the warning time before adding visual complexity.
use_when: Designing or prototyping a timed hazard-dodging game where players must move to safety.
do: Use a consistent warning, danger and safe colour sequence.
Test scoring and movement on a simple grid before producing final artwork.
avoid: Changing safe tiles without advance warning.
Adding decoration that obscures the red and green state colours.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal phygital game GDD, example 1 (course material)

title: Prove competitive body-controlled Snake with simple PC inputs
text: A two-player Snake concept can be tested before building its LED-floor controls: mark P1 and P2 standing positions in the simulation, map P1 to WASD and P2 to the arrow keys, and show both snakes on a simulated projector screen. Eating food lengthens a snake, while hitting its own head-to-body path or another player's tail kills it, creating direct competition through shared space. This cheap setup tests whether steering, growth and collision rules are understandable and fun before investing in physical tracking.
use_when: Prototyping a multiplayer game whose final version uses floor positions or body movement as controls.
do: Give each player a separate, familiar input set.
Display both players and their trails in one shared view.
Test collisions between players as well as self-collisions.
avoid: Building physical tracking before validating the core competitive rules.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal phygital game GDD, example 1 (course material)

title: Use a fail-safe casual round for walk-in groups
text: For children, families and mixed-skill friends, teach the rules within 30 seconds and target rounds of 2 to 5 minutes. Adjust difficulty to the group, make fun more important than ranking, and let mistakes cost points rather than end the run. Confirm every success or error with immediate, distinct colour, sound or animation feedback.
use_when: Shaping a relaxed walk-in game for a family venue or mixed-ability group
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal phygital game GDD, example 1 (course material)

title: Split private MR action from public information
text: Keep the player's attention on physical movement, while placing shared goals, time, scores and results on a wall screen that is visible from every angle. Treat the headset view as a private layer that bystanders cannot see, so spectators need public information plus readable player reactions to follow the game. This supports the useful venue pattern of head up for information and feet down for control.
use_when: Planning information and spectator visibility for an MR venue game
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal phygital game GDD, example 1 (course material)

title: Replace territory control with a visible checkpoint race
text: If a creator asks for Territory War, do not promise floor tiles that change team ownership or a percentage-controlled map. Offer the closest supported contest instead: players walk separate copies of a checkpoint course, with a live leaderboard and results on a shared screen. For a gentler group, use the same course as an individual score challenge without forced ranking.
use_when: A creator requests team territory control or tile-painting competition
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal phygital game GDD, example 1 (course material)

title: Escalate pressure by shrinking safe choices
text: Build difficulty across rounds by reducing safe choices rather than only speeding everything up: start with about 4 safe squares, end with 1, and place later objectives farther away. On hard boards, let the safe opportunity shift so players must read and follow the pattern. In this engine, express this through guard coverage, cracked squares and ordered targets in tactics, or tighter hazard spacing between checkpoints in a runner. Never use objective distance to force running in MR.
use_when: Designing a difficulty curve for a spatial course or board
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

title: Translate HP victory into supported scoring
text: Do not promise HP totals, damage or team elimination: these engines have no general health or combat-result system. Translate 'the side with more HP wins' into supported outcomes: checkpoint +100, hazard -25, finish +300 plus a time bonus, with a leaderboard for races. For MR battle, frame victory as clearing the chapters and defeating the boss rather than comparing team HP.
use_when: A creator asks for health-based team win, loss and tie rules
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

title: Put live race stakes where spectators can watch
text: A responsive floor arena becomes a group event when a big screen shows scores and time live, letting teams and onlookers follow the contest. For an online runner race, use the live leaderboard and place dodges, the last checkpoint and the portal where spectators can see players' bodies. Spectators should cheer or call hints from outside the route, never enter the play area for a task.
use_when: Designing for friends, parties, school groups or team building with people watching.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

title: Make the party-game goal understandable in seconds
text: The venue's broad-age party zone succeeds with games whose rules are understood within a few seconds, whether played alone or in teams. Give a new Land one immediate goal, a visible next action and instant feedback; ordered checkpoint labels can carry the story without a long briefing. Add depth through route, timing and hazard placement rather than stacking extra rules.
use_when: The creator expects mixed ages, first-time players or quick party rotation.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

title: Build one shared spectacle worth remembering
text: The 360-degree arena surrounds several players with one scene and full-view giant creatures, creating both immersion and a photo-worthy memory. Recreate that design beat with a chapter boss, a large beast or a dramatic final portal that everyone can anticipate and witness together. In MR, frame it against the real room and keep it visible to spectators instead of hiding the climax in a private UI moment.
use_when: A group experience needs a clear climax or a memorable highlight beyond scoring.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

title: Walk-in casual play needs instant goals and soft failure
text: For families and friend groups, target a goal players understand within 30 seconds and rounds lasting 2 to 5 minutes. Let mistakes reduce score rather than end the session, reinforce every action with clear colour, sound and animation, and offer adjustable difficulty across varied bright themes. Keep rankings optional and design the same core activity for solo play or parallel group play so competition never blocks relaxed participation.
use_when: A creator wants a relaxed, accessible venue game for mixed ages or walk-in groups.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

title: Telegraph danger, then escalate movement demands
text: A readable movement round can use three distinct states: blinking orange warns for 3 to 5 seconds, green marks safety, and red confirms the hazard. Increase difficulty by shrinking the safe area from 4 grid cells toward 1, placing it progressively farther from players, and reserving a moving safe area for the hardest level. This creates a learnable rhythm before demanding faster or more sustained movement, while immediate feedback keeps failure understandable.
use_when: Designing repeated hazard rounds or a difficulty curve around timed movement.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

title: Size movement and readability to the floor grid
text: The reference play lane is 3 by 6 metres, divided into 10 by 20 cells of 30 by 30 centimetres, with stepping detected and light feedback shown immediately. Use that cell size to judge reachable distances and safe-area capacity, and separate communication by surface: floor colour for actions, a projected wall for prompts and animation, and a monitor for score, time and results. Two identical lanes can support parallel teams without requiring everyone to share one floor.
use_when: Planning a real-floor group game, its information displays, or a two-lane layout.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

title: Lava Escape contrasts forgiving co-op with team survival
text: In a 90-second single-lane version for 2 to 4 players, each timely safe-zone arrival earns 10 points and standing in lava loses 10, so errors never end play. The dual-lane version instead fields 2 teams of 2 to 4, gives each team 10 HP, subtracts HP according to how many members are caught, and awards the win to the team with more HP after 90 seconds. The comparison shows how the same telegraphed activity can shift from forgiving cooperation to optional rivalry by changing scoring, not by changing its basic rules.
use_when: A creator needs cooperative and competitive variants of one short group activity.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

title: Play first, then choose a creative track
text: For a one-day school game-design event, let students sample the medium before asking them to create: allow 20 minutes for orientation, safety and grouping, two 40-minute rotations covering four play stations, then a 20-minute scored group finale. After lunch, give students a choice of game creation, AI video or art, with 105 minutes of hands-on work. This sequence builds shared references in the morning and ownership in the afternoon.
use_when: Designing an educational visit, workshop or event that combines playing games with making student work.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

title: End a student workshop with a visible artifact
text: Keep hands-on school groups to about 12 to 15 students so everyone can contribute. Reserve the final 40 minutes for finishing work and preparing presentations, followed by 20 minutes to screen every track's creations, award certificates and take a group photo. Give students a usable file to take back for a school portfolio; the public finale and take-home artifact make the day feel consequential rather than like an isolated demo.
use_when: Planning the group size, final phase and lasting outcome of a school or youth creation workshop.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

title: Short matches benefit from three genuinely different jobs
text: This casual territory-control example uses a 5 minute, 6 player 3v3 match on a 5.5 x 11.7 m LED floor, with victory going to the larger colored area when time expires. Its roles separate bodily area capture, ranged clearing, and resource planning, so players can contribute through exertion, accuracy, or judgment rather than everyone doing the same task. Use this as a role-clarity reference when discussing group play, then express the desired experience through supported battle, tactics, or runner mechanics.
use_when: A creator wants a short physical team contest with complementary player roles.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground casual mode GDD, example 2 (course material)

title: Autonomous pressure keeps play moving without a leader
text: Spawning 5 soldier minions every 10 seconds gives this territory match a baseline contest even if nobody performs the Commander role. The reusable lesson is to keep the core activity moving without constant input from an organizer or strategist, so a hesitant or absent leader cannot stall everyone's fun. In this engine, preserve that principle with self-running battle enemy chapters or an individually playable runner race rather than units players must command.
use_when: A group concept depends on one confident player directing everyone else.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground casual mode GDD, example 2 (course material)

title: Teach party games in ten seconds
text: For casual venue and party play, aim for a goal players can understand in about 10 seconds. Use one immediately readable objective and let the first attempt teach the interaction, rather than front-loading instructions. This keeps the game approachable for newcomers and workable for both solo sessions and group rotations.
use_when: Designing onboarding for a casual MR game with short rounds or rotating players.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

title: Offer privacy for celebrations and teams
text: Birthdays, private parties and company events benefit from a private play room rather than a shared public floor. Plan a hosted session with staff support throughout, so the group can focus on playing together instead of equipment or etiquette problems. Privacy is itself part of the event value, not merely a venue detail.
use_when: A creator is designing for a birthday, private party, company event or established friend group.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

title: Make breaks part of the social session
text: Schedule a comfortable regrouping point between rounds where players can have snacks and drinks while watching friends continue. Treat it as the group's meeting place, not dead time outside the experience. This supports mixed energy levels and keeps nonplaying friends and families involved.
use_when: Planning a multi-round venue session for friends, families, schools or other groups.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

title: Redirect shooting requests to sword combat
text: A creator inspired by outdoor co-op shooter attractions may ask for controller guns, but the engine cannot provide shooting. Say so kindly and offer MR battle instead: the right controller is a sword, enemies approach slowly from the edges, and players step out of red warning rings before chapters culminate in a boss. This preserves action, fantasy and physical dodging without inventing firearms or team assault mechanics.
use_when: The creator asks for an MR shooter, gun combat or a co-op assault inspired by venue shooter games.
do: Offer the battle genre's close-range sword combat and readable dodge warnings.
Keep cooperative team planning as a discussion goal only if the selected online mode supports the session format.
avoid: Do not promise gun controllers, shooting, or team assault mechanics.
Do not copy an outdoor shooting theme into daylight without considering MR visibility.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

title: Keep versus rounds short, symmetric, and easy to rematch
text: For a friendly head-to-head contest, start with a 60 second round so the result arrives quickly and a rematch feels effortless. Give opponents mirrored or otherwise symmetric starting positions and equivalent opportunities, then make the win condition simply who captured or scored more. If the board is mirrored, count each logical scoring cell only once rather than accidentally doubling one side's territory.
use_when: Designing a fast competitive race, score duel, or other repeatable contest for friends
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

title: Translate territory capture wishes into supported competition
text: When a creator asks to move around and capture territory, do not promise persistent cell ownership, territory control, power-ups, or combat because those mechanics are not available. Offer the closest supported fantasy: a tactics board about capturing targets in order while avoiding guards, or a runner race where players take ordered checkpoints and compare scores on a live leaderboard. Preserve the requested fast, friendly rivalry with short rounds and clear scoring rather than copying the unsupported mechanic.
use_when: A creator describes Territory War, Splatoon-like claiming, or another territory-control game
do: Offer ordered target capture in tactics
Offer an ordered-checkpoint runner race with a leaderboard
Keep the competitive round brief and readable
avoid: Promising cells that remain owned or change ownership
Adding power-ups, combat, or remote multiplayer
Treating mirrored cells as extra scoring cells
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

title: Reuse one core challenge across three session formats
text: Offer distinct ways to frame the same challenge rather than inventing separate mechanics: a 30-second time attack compares how much each player achieves, an endless round continues until stamina runs out, and a tournament uses a bracket for 4 to 8 players. Choose time attack for quick turns and spectators, endless for personal endurance, and a bracket when the group wants a clear overall winner.
use_when: A creator wants replayability, a party format, or several game modes around one core activity.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

title: Prove the core loop before adding content
text: Build in dependency order: first prove control input, movement, and the basic scene, then add round structure such as best-of-3 logic and clear win and lose states. Polish sound, visuals, and assets only after the game is playable, and leave power-ups, obstacles, and extra modes for last. This prevents optional variety from hiding a weak or incomplete core loop.
use_when: Planning a prototype or deciding which requested features belong in the first playable version.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

title: Short duel rounds keep party crowds rotating
text: For a booth or party activation, structure a head-to-head contest as best of 3, with two equal 100 m rounds and a deciding third only if needed. First to 2 round wins takes the match, keeping the full session to 2-3 minutes. Equal goals and frequent resets make the result easy to follow, give a losing player a quick comeback chance, and limit spectator waiting.
use_when: Designing a social race for an event, booth, or party with people waiting to play.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

title: Make physical effort visibly drive progress
text: When exertion is the core input, make the relationship immediate: faster movement produces faster progress, while no movement produces none. Set base speed to 0, scale acceleration with a tunable sensitivity multiplier, and smooth the result with lerp so motion stays readable rather than jittery. Keep the fantasy and on-screen progress aligned so both players and spectators can understand why someone is winning.
use_when: Turning a physical action into speed, score, or another continuous race advantage.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

title: Teach the action before a synchronized race start
text: For an instantly learned party game, wait until both players have joined and are ready, then show one animated instruction that demonstrates the core action. Follow it with a visible 3, 2, 1 countdown so neither player gains an accidental start advantage. During play, show both competitors' progress toward the same finish continuously, making the goal and changing lead readable without further explanation.
use_when: Onboarding first-time players into a short competitive game with one main action.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

title: Settle XR mode, venue, players, and locomotion first
text: Before designing mechanics, establish whether the experience is MR passthrough, VR, or MR with a VR fallback; whether the venue is already calibrated, an ordinary room, or a new space requiring a scan; and whether play is solo, co-located, or remote online. In MR, design for physical walking only and never promise joystick locomotion; reserve joystick movement for VR. These decisions determine the layout, multiplayer model, and fallback experience.
use_when: Starting an XR concept whose display mode, venue, or multiplayer arrangement is still unclear.
do: Record display mode, venue readiness, player configuration, and locomotion at intake
Use real walking as the MR movement assumption and joystick movement only for VR
avoid: Deferring venue or player configuration until after mechanics are designed
Adding joystick locomotion to an MR concept
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

title: Pause and require deliberate resume after headset interruption
text: Treat headset removal or opening the system menu as an immediate game pause, since the player may no longer be able to see hazards or other people. Resume only after the headset is visible again and the player gives a fresh, explicit confirmation; require the previous input to be released first so a held button cannot restart play accidentally. This prevents the game from advancing while the player is disoriented or unattended.
use_when: Designing pause and resume behavior for a headset game, especially one with physical walking or timed hazards.
do: Pause immediately when headset visibility is lost
Require a fresh, deliberate confirmation before resuming
avoid: Letting hazards or timers continue while the player cannot see the game
Allowing a held button to resume play automatically
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

title: Turn a territory-control wish into a supported race
text: A request for competitive territory capture cannot be implemented literally because the engine has no tile ownership or direct player conflict. Offer the closest supported contest: an online runner race where everyone walks or controls their own copy, touches 4 to 10 checkpoints in order, avoids hazards, and competes on a live leaderboard. Preserve the brief, party-friendly rivalry with an optional time limit and the standard score of +100 per checkpoint, -25 per hazard, and +300 for finishing plus a time bonus.
use_when: A creator asks for Territory War, area capture, or direct competitive grid control.
do: Use an online runner race with identical courses and a live leaderboard.
Set a time limit and build the contest around ordered checkpoints, hazards, and finishing.
avoid: Do not promise capturable cells, direct invasion, mirror capture, or grid ownership scoring.
Do not describe the shared-floor option as competitive territory control; it only lets players see avatars.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

title: Use a hard-stop one-minute party round
text: For a quick party competition, a fixed 60-second round creates urgency without demanding a long commitment, and is suitable for an audience aged 8+. Keep the timer visible, end exactly at zero instead of inventing overtime, and define the tie result explicitly so the winner announcement is never ambiguous. In a runner design, pair the time limit with a simple published scoring rule so players understand whether to prioritize checkpoints, hazard avoidance, or a fast finish.
use_when: Designing a short local or online competition for casual players, families, or groups.
do: Keep the objective to one sentence and the countdown visible.
State whether equal scores produce a draw before play begins.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

title: Use symmetry to keep short duels fair and legible
text: Symmetric competition makes fairness and relative progress easy to read: mirrored sides provide equivalent routes and starting conditions, while a blocked center initially separates rivals and an open center creates a more aggressive risk-versus-reward variant. If an action duplicates progress elsewhere, count each logical objective only once; the source scores just half its 10 by 6 grid for this reason. For a supported race, use identical course copies and a live leaderboard rather than implementing capture mirroring.
use_when: Structuring a two-player contest or explaining why identical race courses and nonduplicated scoring matter.
do: Give competitors the same layout, start conditions, and scoring opportunities.
Explain any mirroring or duplication rule visually before scoring begins.
avoid: Do not award points twice for mirrored or otherwise duplicated progress.
Do not rely on spectators or players inferring a hidden symmetry rule.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

title: Compose MR around the visible real venue
text: In passthrough MR, treat the real room as the backdrop: do not add a sky, cover the real floor with an opaque virtual floor, apply a full-screen tint, or float objects without a clear physical reason. Let real walls occlude virtual objects so the scene feels grounded, and keep all decorative content switchable as one group when a venue needs an unobstructed view.
use_when: Planning the visual composition and decoration of a passthrough MR game
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

title: Keep MR feedback clear without moving the headset view
text: Never shake or move the XR camera for impact feedback; use controller haptics and brief HUD flashes instead. Keep large flashes and dust effects at opacity 0.6 or below, and fade particles within 0.6 m of the head so they cannot obscure the player's view of real surroundings.
use_when: Choosing impact, hazard, and celebration feedback for a walking MR experience
do: Use haptics and HUD flashes for hits or impacts
Cap large effect opacity at 0.6
Fade particles closer than 0.6 m to the head
avoid: Camera shake in the headset
Effects that hide real walls, people, or obstacles
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

title: Scale MR creatures against real human bodies
text: Build MR scenes at 1:1 scale, with one world unit equal to one metre, and judge sizes against the player's actual body rather than a desktop screen. As a useful upper range, humanoid enemies should be no taller than about 2.1 m and bosses around 2.7 m, preserving drama without making nearby creatures overwhelmingly large.
use_when: Setting character, enemy, and prop dimensions for a room-scale MR game
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

title: Use short race sets with clear comeback stakes
text: For a party race session, a best-of-3 set gives players a concrete comeback arc without requiring a long campaign: announce each round winner and score, then reserve the champion celebration for the final result. A 2-1 finish feels meaningfully different from a single isolated win. In this engine, run the set as three separate races rather than promising built-in rounds, and offer replay immediately after the champion screen.
use_when: Designing a repeatable competitive party session for friends or families
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

title: Separate personal progress from shared race status
text: A head-to-head race is easiest to follow when each player has a distinct personal view, while comparative progress and the match score occupy one consistent shared location. Keep secondary measures such as depth at the side so they do not compete with the main question of who is ahead. On PC this can be left and right views with central progress; in MR, put the shared comparison on a spectator leaderboard because bystanders cannot see the virtual course.
use_when: Prototyping the HUD or spectator presentation for a two-player race
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

title: High-contrast neon versus palette
text: For a cyberpunk competitive prototype, use a dark purple-blue background (#0a0a1a to #16213e), neon red-pink (#ff0055) for Player 1, neon cyan (#00d4ff) for Player 2, gray (#333333) for neutral elements, and neon green (#00ff9f) for UI accents. Pair uppercase, letter-spaced monospace type with restrained motion: 0.5-second screen fades, 1-second timer and player pulses, a 2-second start-button pulse, and a 3-4-second title gradient cycle. In MR, favor this dark neon treatment indoors or after dark so daylight does not wash it out.
use_when: Creating key art, a HUD mockup, or visual identity for a head-to-head neon arena concept.
do: Keep player colors consistent across markers, scores, and previews.
Reserve green for interface accents rather than a third player.
Test neon readability under the actual venue lighting.
avoid: Using glow as the only way to distinguish players.
Assuming dark neon scenes remain readable in bright daylight.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

title: Fast competitive HUD and retry loop
text: Storyboard a short competitive game as start screen, game screen, game over, then play again. The start screen should combine mode selection, player and control previews, a rules summary, and one large start action; during a 60-second round, keep the timer and both live scores above the playfield and control hints below it. End by naming the winner, showing both scores, and offering restart, so a loss leads directly to another attempt.
use_when: Prototyping a timed score contest where players must understand controls and standings at a glance.
do: Show controls before play and keep them available during play.
Place timer and scores outside the main action area.
Make restart the primary game-over action.
avoid: Hiding rules or controls on a separate screen.
Letting animated titles compete with the timer and scores for attention.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

title: Redirect territory-control wishes
text: A creator asking for territory war may mean tile capture on entry, mirrored ownership, and two players sharing one keyboard; do not promise those mechanics. Offer battle chapters with distinct enemies and a boss for direct conflict, or a timed tactics board with ordered target captures and guard avoidance for spatial planning. If the real wish is score rivalry, use a race with a live leaderboard, while retaining red-versus-cyan arena styling as theme rather than unsupported territory mechanics.
use_when: A creator asks for territory capture, local versus control, or a game modeled on this grid arena.
do: Identify whether the wish is combat, spatial planning, or score rivalry.
Map the wish to battle, tactics, or an online race respectively.
Preserve the versus fantasy through color and presentation.
avoid: Promising tile ownership, shared-keyboard multiplayer, or grid-capture rules.
Calling ordered tactics targets territorial control.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

title: Give MR players a real escape window
text: Telegraph area attacks for at least 1.3 seconds because a walking player needs roughly 1 second to move after seeing a signal. Make the warning ring match the damage area exactly, leave empty floor around it for escape, hold new attacks when the player is near a real wall or boundary, and never use knockback or forced movement. Warn about threats from behind with a screen-edge arrow and spatial audio rather than a full-screen tint.
use_when: Designing MR attacks, hazards, or boss patterns that require physical dodging.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

title: Budget XR visuals for the worst combat frame
text: Do not base XR art direction on bloom or other post-processing, and disable shadows unless they are essential. Measure representative content before setting budgets, then test the densest case, such as a boss with all enemies and debris, and ensure no instanced batch overflows. Proven starting references are at most 40 meshes and 6k triangles for a boss, 12 draw calls for effects, and 40 monsters distributed across 8 instanced batches.
use_when: Choosing enemy counts, boss complexity, and effects for a Quest XR battle.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

title: Build a desktop preview for fast design checks
text: Give every XR project a desktop preview with walking, aiming or interaction, a third-person camera, and explicit start and restart controls. Include autoplay for demos and captures, visible fps, draw-call and particle counts, opt-in invulnerability for testing only, and controls that isolate one enemy type or model. These tools make pacing, readability, and worst-case behavior inspectable without putting on a headset for every check.
use_when: Prototyping or debugging an XR game and preparing demonstrations.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

title: A passing build is not a playable game
text: Verify the real play flow from entry through start, actions, damage, HUD updates, turns, and restart while checking performance and errors. Inspect every real-time capture visually, because automated tests can pass while the scene is unattractive, unreadable, or effectively unplayable. Before calling work finished, state plainly which features have not yet been tested in an actual headset.
use_when: Validating a prototype before presenting it as complete to a creator.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

title: Ask one decision-changing question at a time
text: Interview the creator one question at a time, offer answer chips, and briefly explain why each answer matters. Ask when the goal is ambiguous or the answer would change the design; act when confident, stop when the brief is complete, and confirm the brief before designing. This elicits more useful preferences with less creator effort than an open prompt box.
use_when: Starting a vague brief or deciding whether another clarification is worth asking
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Differentiate three options on explicit design axes
text: Offer three genuinely different games, not cosmetic variants, and make their differences explicit on axes such as core play, pacing, social fit, venue demands, and intended feelings. Give each option reasons, risks, four scores, and an AI recommendation, but let the creator choose, modify, or remix. Explicit axes reduce design fixation, while a small structured set avoids choice overload.
use_when: Turning a confirmed brief into design choices without steering the creator toward near-duplicates
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Approve a concrete prototype before building
text: Before building, show key art, a storyboard, the player flow, a palette, and a code-drawn level sketch, then revise from creator comments until approval. Measure time to approval and compare the finished build with the approved prototype. These checks reveal whether the prototype communicates quickly and whether implementation quietly drifts from the agreed design.
use_when: The creator needs to understand and approve the game before implementation
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Turn intended feelings into the evaluation target
text: Record target players, context, session length, and intended feelings using the eight MDA aesthetics, then reuse those feelings as the evaluation target rather than treating them as mood words. Have persona bots walk the level and a judge check it against the brief, followed by a study with people. This tests whether the built game delivers the agreed experience, not merely whether it is valid.
use_when: Checking whether a completed design still fulfills its experiential brief
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Put triangle detail where players see it
text: For real-time XR art, budget about 15,000 to 25,000 triangles for a hero character, 3,000 to 6,000 for ordinary monsters, and under 250,000 for the whole scene. Spend triangles on curved silhouettes and shaded contours rather than flat surfaces, then review front, side, top and back captures before approval. This reserves detail for readable forms instead of invisible surface density.
use_when: Planning or reviewing the visual asset scope for a real-time game
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

title: Prototype beautiful heroes before promising them
text: A reusable low-poly toon kit is a good fit for enemy groups, bosses and scene props, but it is not a safe basis for promising a cute or beautiful game-render-quality lead. When hero beauty matters to the creator, commission or generate a visual prototype first and approve that target before producing the cast. This exposes the fidelity gap early rather than after the production style is locked.
use_when: A creator asks for exceptionally attractive or cute lead characters
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

title: Make every strike produce local hit feedback
text: Every object that can be struck should support a visible emissive flash, with independently controllable materials whenever characters must react separately. Shared materials can otherwise make several characters flash as one and blur which target was hit. A brief flash on the struck character gives immediate, local confirmation without adding extra UI.
use_when: Designing readable feedback for melee hits or other strikes
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

title: Hand over headset evidence, not assumed readiness
text: With each headset prototype, provide a link that works on the target device, step-by-step controls, captures from the running build, and fps, draw-call and triangle figures when available. State plainly what has and has not been tested in the headset. A localhost link only works on the host computer, so headset review needs a deployed link.
use_when: Preparing a playable XR prototype for creator review or playtesting
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

title: Echo player mistakes on the spectator display
text: Give spectators a dedicated visual reaction when a player triggers an important event, such as a glass ornament shattering when that player breaks a floor cell. Keep the effect decorative so it cannot alter gameplay, and make it brief and readable: shards can fall for 0.7 seconds and travel 0.6 metres before a fresh ornament appears after 1.5 seconds. Varying the motion and which ornament reacts keeps repeated events lively while preserving the cause-and-effect link.
use_when: Designing a screen or viewing area for people watching a floor or room-scale game
do: Trigger the spectator effect directly from the real gameplay event
Use a short, exaggerated animation that reads from a distance
Reset decorations quickly so later events remain visible
avoid: Letting decorative effects change the game state
Using identical, mechanical motion for every repeated effect
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Use short rounds with explicit breathers
text: For an active group score chase, start from 3 rounds of 60 seconds, an 8 second break between rounds, and a 3 second countdown before play. The breaks create a clear rhythm for checking scores and recovering without ending the session, while the countdown prevents a confusing start. Treat these as playtest defaults rather than fixed rules.
use_when: Structuring session length and pacing for a physically active score-chasing game.
do: Show a countdown before each round.
Use inter-round pauses for recovery and score feedback.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Align reward tiers with rarity and celebrate real pickups
text: Make value readable through a consistent visual ladder: in this design, six common bounties score 1 point, while the rarer most-wanted target scores 5. Bronze marks common rewards, silver the temporarily enlarged reward, and gold the rarest and most valuable. Play the coin-flip celebration only when a player actually collects a reward, not when it expires or is cleared, so the effect confirms player success rather than visual noise.
use_when: Designing collectible value, score readability, and collection feedback.
do: Tie the strongest visual tier to the rarest high-value reward.
Reserve pickup animation for the player-triggered collection path.
avoid: Do not use success animation for expiry or teardown.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Space pickups beyond double their collection reach
text: For position-based collection, keep item centres farther apart than twice the combined grab reach, or one standing position may collect two items. With a combined reach of 0.62 m, the danger threshold is 1.24 m: a 1.2 m minimum gap caused accidental double pickups, while 1.6 m provided reliable separation. Use the same reach-plus-margin calculation whenever spawn spacing is tuned.
use_when: Placing floor collectibles or other proximity-triggered rewards that should be collected individually.
do: Calculate spacing from the combined player and item collection radii.
Add margin above twice that reach.
avoid: Do not set minimum spacing just below the double-collection threshold.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Give every input path the same brief button punch
text: Use one button-feedback pattern whether activation comes from a mouse, LED floor, or another input route. A useful tuning is a 0.15 scale punch over 0.25 seconds with vibrato 6, returning automatically to the original scale so Start, Restart, and Exit remain pressable. If a button also has an idle breathing pulse, suspend and restart that pulse around the punch instead of letting both animations fight over scale.
use_when: Prototyping responsive menus or floor-operated controls that must remain reusable.
do: Route all input methods through equivalent press feedback.
Keep reusable controls visible and pressable after activation.
avoid: Do not let idle and press animations compete for the same scale.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Make tracked movement stable before tying gameplay to it
text: For a floor-positioned MR game, treat live positions as noisy: smooth the signal, ignore movements below about 0.03 m, and start with roughly 0.15 s of smoothing to reduce visible jitter. Reject implausible jumps and poses outside calibrated bounds, hold the last good position during brief signal gaps, then recover gradually rather than teleporting; useful starting limits are a 1 s pose age, 1 m bounds margin, and 2 m snap threshold. Playtest walking, stopping, and tracking loss, since sliding or sudden corrections can make checkpoint and hazard outcomes feel unfair.
use_when: Designing or testing MR gameplay whose checkpoints, hazards, or movement depend on tracked player positions.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Handle tracked player loss without breaking the group
text: Give each of the 2 to 4 players a stable slot and an explicit measured, predicted, or lost state with an input age. When tracking is lost, stop that player's ready state, cursor, answers, and attacks without pausing or reassigning everyone else; on recovery, require fresh input rather than replaying stale actions. Never let bots silently replace real tracking, and reset readiness and session state between rounds.
use_when: Building a multiplayer floor tracked game where players can drop out, reconnect, or remain still between rounds
do: Display tracking loss and recovery clearly to players and operators
Require a fresh ready action after reconnecting or starting a new round
avoid: Refreshing a player's acceptance or readiness from an old frame
Reassigning identities when somebody reconnects
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Make every supported player count a complete game
text: For selectable 2, 3, or 4 player sessions, build menus, playfields, and results from the chosen roster instead of discovering whoever happens to be in the scene. Check that every active player has an independent cursor, score, hit or answer grading, and a way to win or tie, while unused slots stay excluded. Use count dependent layouts and explicit physical progress units, for example two lanes per player in a path game, so adding players does not merely squeeze a two player screen.
use_when: Designing a game with variable group size, shared cursors, competitive scoring, or count dependent layouts
do: Playtest 2, 3, and 4 player sessions independently
Include ties and missing players in results-screen playtests
avoid: Squeezing additional players into a fixed two player layout
Allowing inactive slots to score, answer, or appear in results
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Prove physical tracking separately from gameplay
text: Prototype a tracked floor game with known metre points at the centre and corners, then test dropouts, long stalls, implausible jumps, and one tag disappearing while the others keep moving. Replay the same recorded cases before changing smoothing or jump thresholds, and keep prediction bounded. Mouse or bot play can validate menus and UI, and synthetic geometry can validate mapping, but neither proves real radio tracking accuracy.
use_when: Turning a screen based prototype into a location tracked physical game
do: Keep labelled recorded tracking cases for repeatable playtests
Check both coordinate mapping and real hardware behavior before promising reliable movement
avoid: Treating successful mouse or bot play as validation of physical tracking
Retuning several tracking thresholds without a repeatable comparison
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Use an automatic Ready-to-countdown onboarding beat
text: When players cannot pause with a keyboard, let the start press open a short Ready hold, then begin the 3-2-1 countdown automatically rather than chaining straight into play. Keep every in-round instruction, including Ready and prompts such as Walk, in one consistent headline position, and reveal hidden solution information only when the Memorize phase actually starts. This gives players a predictable moment to orient themselves without letting them study the answer early.
use_when: Designing the start and memorize phases of a movement or memory game with limited input
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Finish outcome effects before the judging beat ends
text: Budget the complete failure or success animation inside the state that displays it: in this project, all crack and shard runtime had to stay comfortably below the 1.3 second judging window. Do not merely start an effect at judgment and advance the state machine on a fixed timer, or the transition will cut it off. Treat the judging duration as an audiovisual budget and shorten or simplify effects when necessary.
use_when: Timing breakage, scoring, or other outcome effects between rounds
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Separate player identity, game state, and surface decoration
text: Give each player a hollow ring with a solid inner circle, and reuse that player's inner-circle color in their progress display so identity remains consistent across the HUD. On grid cells, place beveled borders and gloss beneath a live gameplay tint for hidden, safe, breaking, broken, or wrong states. Decoration can make surfaces feel like glass, but the state color must remain the top readability layer.
use_when: Building readable player cursors and state-heavy floor or board cells
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Keep MR sword combat grounded and visually clear
text: For an MR battle, make the right controller the sword: a fast swing attacks, real steps dodge red danger rings, and the trigger restarts after a run. Place the arena beneath the player's feet and align it with their initial view so the goal is immediately understandable. Hide tall decorative objects such as pillars and thrones in MR, leaving the floor and enemies readable against passthrough surroundings.
use_when: Designing the interaction and arena presentation for a Quest 3 passthrough battle game.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

title: Escalate a battle boss without losing dodge readability
text: Give the boss a clear targeted ground slam, then intensify the same pattern below half health by adding 3 extra warning rings and summoning weak grunts. This creates a readable second phase: the player already understands the main threat, while added rings test positioning and grunts divide attention. Keep the new pressure telegraphed rather than introducing an unrelated surprise attack.
use_when: Designing or tuning a PC battle boss and its chapter climax
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder PC battle engine (Vite + three.js template)

title: Make battle defense readable on the ground
text: Build PC sword combat around a 3-hit combo whose third strike deals double damage, plus a dash on Space or right click that evades attacks.
