Assume most children are new to VR, use immediate one-action onboarding, keep the counter out of the cleared route, and show the live leaderboard to parents and people waiting. A mascot that cannot converse can still welcome players and cheer at the start and finish. Plan VR for ages 10 and up, with close adult supervision for younger children.
use_when: Designing a high-throughput MR booth for children, families, and passing spectators.
do: Target a 3-minute solo round with immediate onboarding
Show the leaderboard to parents and the queue
Use the mascot as a nonverbal greeter and cheerleader
avoid: Using a long tutorial for first-time young players
Making the mascot converse when the engine cannot support dialogue
Hiding the score from the queue
source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

title: Explain follow-ups and confirm the brief before designing
text: Keep a fixed set of required design fields, but make follow-up questions adaptive and briefly explain why each non-obvious question matters. End the interview with a one-screen brief covering concept, players, group size, VR experience, intended feelings, venue or environment, session length and play mode, then require an explicit confirmation or edit. Never request personal data while trying to fill design gaps.
use_when: Starting a creator interview or deciding whether enough information exists to propose games
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Set intended feelings before choosing mechanics
text: Choose the intended player experience early, using the 8 MDA aesthetics: sensation, fantasy, narrative, challenge, fellowship, discovery, expression and submission. Designers reason from mechanics toward aesthetics, but players encounter the resulting feelings first, so record the aesthetic goals before selecting a genre or mechanic. Reuse those goals later as criteria for judging generated content and alternatives, with fellowship especially relevant to group play.
use_when: Turning a creator's broad wish into design goals or evaluating whether options preserve the desired experience
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Offer three genuinely different options with visible trade-offs
text: Present three options, each with a pitch, core loop, player and venue fit, risks, scores for fun, player fit, platform fit and buildability, plus one recommendation. Declare different design axes such as dominant aesthetic, core mechanic and social structure, and verify that the options differ on at least two axes so they do not collapse into one game with three skins. A small set suits non-experts comparing complex whole-game concepts, while alternatives also elicit more critical feedback and reduce fixation better than a single proposal.
use_when: Generating concept choices for a non-expert creator
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Keep the creator in charge of the AI recommendation
text: The AI may recommend one option, but the creator makes the final choice and can request changes before anything is built. Explain how every score was derived rather than showing bare numbers, because scores and recommendations can induce acceptance even when the advice is wrong. Where over-reliance is a concern, ask the creator to state an initial preference before revealing the AI recommendation, while accepting that this extra step may feel less smooth.
use_when: Presenting scores and a recommended concept without letting the AI quietly take over the decision
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Require fresh input after an MR interruption
text: When a player removes the headset or the session pauses, do not resume movement or attacks from a button that was already held. Wait until every control is released, then require a new press so the game cannot continue acting on its own while the player is disoriented.
use_when: Designing pause, resume, or headset removal behavior for a physically played MR game
do: Clear held input on pause and require release followed by a fresh press on resume
Playtest interruptions while movement or attack controls are held
avoid: Resuming immediately from the input state captured before the interruption
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

title: Separate enemy roles by silhouette, not recoloring
text: Give each enemy type a distinct silhouette so players can read its role at a glance, and reserve palette swaps for elemental variants, teams, or skins of the same type. A small role named palette can keep colors consistent across a cast, with emissive accents limited to focal details such as eyes or a core.
use_when: Creating key art or a model palette for a game with several enemy roles and themed variants
do: Test enemy recognition as solid black silhouettes
Reuse one shape with themed colors only when its gameplay role stays the same
avoid: Making different enemy roles differ only by color
Adding glow everywhere instead of using it to mark focal details
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

title: Compare parallel concepts before refining one
text: Develop several concepts in parallel before investing in one detailed design. Research on parallel prototyping links it to better design results, greater divergence, and increased self-efficacy, so use the creator's comparison and critique to reveal preferences. Keep each alternative quick to assess, then refine the chosen direction.
use_when: A creator has a broad brief and needs to choose a game direction without becoming anchored to the first proposal.
do: Make the alternatives differ in a consequential design dimension, not just theme or naming
Ask the creator to compare the options before converging on one
avoid: Presenting three superficial variations of one idea as meaningful alternatives
Refining the first generated concept before the creator has compared directions
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Clarify only ambiguity that changes the design
text: When a brief is vague, ask the clarification whose answer would most change the design, rather than running through a full questionnaire. Work on eliciting preferences and selectively clarifying ambiguous questions supports using dialogue to expose consequential unknowns. For low-impact gaps, state a provisional assumption and keep the conversation moving.
use_when: A creator gives an ambiguous or incomplete request and the next useful question is unclear.
do: Identify ambiguity that would materially change the experience or its feasibility
State provisional assumptions for minor details and invite correction
avoid: Using a long questionnaire to resolve every uncertainty
Asking detailed questions whose answers would not change the proposed game
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Use deliberate variation to counter design fixation
text: Treat polished AI-generated concepts as prompts, not as evidence that the right direction has been found. Research on generative AI and design fixation makes deliberate divergence important: vary a fundamental design dimension between proposals and ask the creator what possibility is missing. This prevents surface-level variations from masquerading as exploration.
use_when: The first generated proposal looks convincing and subsequent ideas are beginning to resemble it.
do: Change a core mechanic, player role, or experience goal between alternatives
Ask what direction is absent before selecting a concept
avoid: Letting visual polish make the first proposal feel settled
Generating more ideas without changing their underlying design assumptions
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Build the mission and route before the scenery
text: Generate a level in two stages: first turn the brief and intended feelings into a mission, ordered objectives and playable route, then dress that route with theme and scenery. This keeps decoration from determining play and makes failures easier to locate: repair the mission or route before adjusting visual layout.
use_when: Turning a creative brief into a playable level layout
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Separate meaningful level design from geometric placement
text: Let the design model specify relations such as before, beside, visible from and clear of, while a solver places objects and enforces geometry. Well-formed output does not prove a meaningful or playable level, so validate semantics separately and use a path-planning agent to test reachability and walkability on the actual MR floor plan. Track schema failures, rule violations and meaning failures separately rather than treating every rejection as the same problem.
use_when: Generating and validating layouts for a real play space
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Playtest with contrasting personas and brief-based targets
text: Create 4 to 6 personas from the intended audience and play styles, such as curious child, cautious parent with child, goal-rusher and wanderer, then run at least 30 seeded simulations per persona per level. Fit walking speed and dwell time to a few real headset traces, and measure completion, session time against the brief, area coverage, idle or lost time, crowding, near-misses, boundary clearance and checkpoint reachability. Judge success against the original players, target session and intended feelings, not merely whether the level can be completed.
use_when: Evaluating a generated MR level before inviting players
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Measure whether generated options truly offer different games
text: Do not assume three proposals are meaningfully different because their themes differ. Plot the three options, and outputs across many briefs, on two-dimensional comparisons such as pacing against spatial spread, then check whether options separate and different briefs produce different level shapes. Use the results to revise generation toward genuinely distinct play experiences.
use_when: Presenting divergent design options to a creator
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Preserve creator agency when scoring options
text: Let the creator rank or choose among design options before revealing the AI's preferred option, so the recommendation does not anchor their judgment. Show what each score is derived from and explicitly mark uncertain scores rather than presenting a bare number. Allow remixing, such as taking the mechanic from option B and the theme from option A, then regenerate the combined design.
use_when: Presenting and comparing AI-generated game concepts with a creator.
do: Let the creator rank or select options before revealing the AI recommendation.
Explain each score's inputs, flag uncertainty, and record acceptance or override rates.
Support combinations such as the mechanic from one option and the theme from another, then regenerate.
avoid: Leading with the AI recommendation and anchoring the creator.
Showing unexplained scores as if they were certain.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Approve a complete paper prototype before building
text: After the creator picks a concept and before building, make a paper prototype with a logline, 3 design pillars, a 4 to 6 colour palette, key art, a 3 to 4 panel session storyboard, screen contents, minute-by-minute flow, and a top-down level sketch. Add 2 to 4 questions that a later playtest must answer. Revise as often as needed from creator comments, keep every version, and require the build plan to follow the approved prototype.
use_when: Turning a selected game option into an agreed, buildable design.
do: Prepare a logline, three pillars, visual direction, storyboard, flow, level sketch, and playtest questions.
Revise from creator comments and retain each version.
Make the approved prototype the contract for the build plan.
avoid: Building a playable level before the experience has been agreed.
Omitting the playtest questions or allowing the build to drift from approval.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Do not let the first image choose the game
text: Keep the initial game options text-only so an attractive generated picture does not decide which concept the creator selects. Once prototyping begins, treat key art as a cheap visual hypothesis and drive revisions from the creator's comments rather than attachment to the first image. This preserves exploration of visual directions while letting the creator judge experience goals before production geometry.
use_when: Using text-to-image generation during concept selection or visual prototyping.
do: Keep initial concept comparisons text-only.
Treat generated key art as a disposable visual hypothesis.
Generate alternatives when comments reveal a different desired experience.
avoid: Attaching generated images to the initial options.
Treating the first attractive image as a settled art direction.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Generate the MR route from the real venue
text: For room-scale passthrough MR, treat the real venue as visible game context and change only the floor layer. Put the venue's size, indoor or outdoor status, lighting, walls, and spectators into the design brief, then fit the route to the detected walkable floor while keeping clear of walls and using the available area. Real walking is the only locomotion, so every path and interaction must remain reachable within that actual room.
use_when: Designing a passthrough MR game for a specific physical room or venue.
do: Gather size, indoor or outdoor setting, light, walls, and spectator presence.
Generate content on detected walkable floor and fit the route to that room.
Use real surroundings as visible context while replacing only the floor.
avoid: Assuming the virtual world can hide the venue.
Adding joystick locomotion or placing content outside the walkable floor.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Capture the venue as structured play data
text: Before laying out an MR game, record walls, exits, obstacles, spectator zones and lighting as structured data rather than a prose description. Snap content to real planes and adapt placement to the room's physical and social context, because site conditions shape play and plane snapping makes placement faster and better. Keep real people and objects visible: this improves usability with little loss of immersion.
use_when: Turning an MR venue description into a playable layout
do: Ask for walls, exits, obstacles, spectator positions and light conditions.
Use real walls, views and audiences as part of the scene.
avoid: Inventing a replacement virtual room when the real room can support play.
Treating venue notes as unstructured flavor text.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Give spectators a deliberate viewing plan
text: MR spectators see players' bodies but not the virtual floor, so add a spectator plan to both the brief and the build. Specify where they stand, provide a shared screen view such as a leaderboard or floor projection, and stage dodges and finishes where their reactions are easy to read. Friends and parents can cheer or call hints, but never assign them a task inside the play area.
use_when: Designing an MR game that friends, parents or an audience will watch
do: Choose a safe spectator zone outside the route.
Make important player actions visible without seeing the headset view.
Use a shared display for game state or results.
avoid: Placing spectators inside the walking course.
Assuming bystanders can understand play from the virtual action alone.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Budget walking comfort and bystander safety
text: Real walking gives more natural movement and presence than walking-in-place or flying, so keep it but budget session length, route length, rest points and stricter limits for children; screen comfort with the SSQ when testing. Keep routes 1.2 m clear, content off real obstacles and at least 0.6 m from area edges, with no sudden scares or fast walking while looking up. Warn about nearby bystanders with combined audio and visual distance cues, which work better than either cue alone.
use_when: Setting MR route length, session duration and safety behavior
do: Include rest points and child-appropriate session limits.
Playtest fatigue, dizziness and route clearance.
Pair visual proximity warnings with audio.
avoid: Maximizing walking distance to make an experience feel substantial.
Using surprise effects that could trigger running.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Let code verify geometry while the model designs meaning
text: Have the model generate layout candidates inside a schema and external validation loop rather than asking it to verify its own spatial reasoning. Build in two stages, route first and scenery second outside a computed keep-clear corridor, with code auto-fixing small geometry slips and at most 2 feedback-driven repair rounds. This division matters: LLM-only repairs reduced blocking objects only from 38 to 30 to 24, while code fixed them in one pass.
use_when: Building or repairing an AI-generated MR floor layout
do: Validate structure and gameplay meaning externally.
Reserve a clear corridor before placing decoration.
Cap model repair rounds at 2 and let code handle deterministic fixes.
avoid: Relying on repeated self-critique to solve precise geometry.
Placing scenery before the route is verified.
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Use bots to rank levels, not replace players
text: Treat automated playtesting as decision support: correlate bot and judge predictions with real players on the same levels before trusting them. An LLM judge can score intended aesthetics plus player and venue fit, using randomized option order, several samples or models with agreement reported, length caps, and independent checking rather than unchecked self-judging. Compute safety as a hard gate from telemetry, never as an LLM opinion.
use_when: Using simulated players or LLM judges to evaluate and revise a generated level
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Playtest the intended feeling at the venue
text: Compare the revised level against the unrevised version with players in the actual venue, and ask directly whether they felt each intended feeling. Use PXI as the main experience scale rather than GEQ, whose factor structure did not replicate; measure sickness with SSQ before and after. In MR passthrough, interpret presence items about realness carefully, and keep questionnaires short: in-headset items can change response variance without changing means.
use_when: Planning an experience playtest, especially for an MR game in its real venue
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Make child playtests short, consented and observable
text: Obtain parental consent and the child's own assent, secure ethics approval first, and allow either to stop the session at any time. Keep sessions short, screen for sickness, use pictorial short-form questions, and include parent observation. Do not rely on an adult's consent or questionnaire responses alone to infer that a child is comfortable.
use_when: Playtesting a game with children or family groups
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Keep the creator in control of AI recommendations
text: Make alternatives differ on explicitly declared axes and verify that difference, so the creator avoids fixation on minor variations of one idea. Explain the basis of scores and recommendations. Let the creator rank the options before revealing the AI's preferred pick, reducing over-reliance while preserving a useful recommendation.
use_when: Presenting AI-generated game options or recommending one direction to a creator
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

title: Define a session policy for lost player tracking
text: For a tracked multiplayer MR session, decide in advance what happens when a required player is lost: pause the session initially, preserve their last visible position if useful, and remove them from actions, collisions, and scoring. Add a grace period only after measuring real tracking losses, rather than letting stale positions affect play. This keeps races and shared-floor sessions fair and avoids unsafe confusion around a stationary avatar.
use_when: Designing multiplayer MR play where tracking loss could disrupt safety or scoring
do: Pause when a required player loses tracking
Exclude lost players from scoring and interactions
Tune grace periods from measured session data
avoid: Letting stale positions keep scoring or colliding
Inventing a grace period before real measurements
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Verify shared MR tracking with real players
text: Before promising a shared-floor MR game, test the full intended player count with independent tracked people, not bots or keyboard substitutes. Simulated fallbacks can hide a failed real-player lookup, while a healthy global signal can hide one rejected player, so monitor connection, last valid update, and position validity per player. Repeat the test after reconnects and roster changes, with explicit recovery when tracking is lost.
use_when: Prototyping or playtesting multiplayer MR with tracked players
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Design the active roster before multiplayer play
text: Define the actual active roster separately from technical capacity: for a 2 to 4 player game, give every participant a stable slot and a unique physical tracker identity. Size ready screens, play lanes and result attribution for that roster, and explicitly test three players as well as two and four so an odd-sized group does not expose silent bot substitution or layout assumptions.
use_when: Planning or playtesting a tracked multiplayer floor game
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Make tracking loss a fair game state
text: For each player, specify what missing, predicted and invalid position input means during play instead of treating one latest position as proof that everyone is tracked. Decide what silence does, such as pausing that player rather than registering steps or failures, and test dropout and recovery with real bodies before accepting the design.
use_when: Defining movement rules and failure handling for physical tracking
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Choose floor triggers and test bodily interference
text: Choose explicitly whether an action requires a foot press, remaining in a tracked spot for a dwell, or a test-only input; clear action state at each round and define whether LED feedback should hold. On site, test simultaneous players, path crossings, occlusions, dropouts and recovery, and record measured update rate, latency and position error rather than trusting configuration values.
use_when: Prototyping tracked floor interactions or multiplayer movement
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Test tracked groups with simulated players disabled
text: For a tracked group game, verify every player slot with a real participant before judging movement, pacing, or lane balance. In Deepspace, slots P3 to P6 silently became bots moving at 1.7 m/s whenever a real pose was unavailable, so a full-looking six-player test could hide broken tracking. Use stable player-to-tracker assignments, check each participant individually, and keep simulated players as an explicit test mode rather than an invisible fallback.
use_when: Preparing or playtesting an MR game with several tracked participants
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Make tracking loss visibly fail safe
text: Treat missing, stale, or out-of-area tracking as unavailable input, not as a valid position at the nearest edge. Clamped coordinates and automatic fallback actors can make the game appear responsive while outcomes no longer match the player's body. Pause scoring and hazard consequences for that player, show a clear tracking-loss state, and resume only after their position is valid again; a connected receiver alone does not prove that every player is tracked.
use_when: Designing recovery and feedback for body-tracked MR play
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Stage the boss entrance before play begins
text: Give a boss fight a short, unambiguous opening beat: the portal grows from zero to full size, the boss emerges, the portal shrinks away, and only then does play begin. A one-time entrance separates anticipation from action, makes the boss arrival memorable, and prevents players from mistaking the introduction for a moment when they should already react.
use_when: Designing the opening presentation and readiness cue for a battle game's boss encounter.
do: Play the portal opening and boss emergence once per fight
Delay active play until the entrance has finished
Close the portal by shrinking it to mark the transition into play
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Start boss rosters equal, then tune by feel
text: For repeated boss fights, select from a boss roster with weighted randomness so encounters vary without requiring new mechanics. Start with equal weights, test each boss individually, then adjust frequencies only after learning which encounters deserve to appear more or less often; weights alter relative likelihood, not a guaranteed fraction over a few sessions.
use_when: Choosing how often different bosses appear across repeated battle sessions.
avoid: Treating a weight as a guaranteed appearance percentage
Tuning roster frequency before every boss has been tested individually
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Treat tracking loss as a participation state
text: When a player's position stops updating, freezing their avatar is not enough: scoring, hazards and other rules may still act on the stale position. Mark that player explicitly unavailable, pause or exclude their participation according to one consistent policy, and preserve their identity when tracking returns rather than silently assigning another input source. This matters most in shared-floor or competitive play, where a dropout must not create an unfair hit, score or ownership change.
use_when: Designing multiplayer play where player positions can drop out or become stale
do: Expose unavailable as an explicit player state
Use one consistent pause or exclusion policy
Restore the same player identity on recovery
avoid: Letting stale coordinates keep scoring
Silently switching a player to another input source
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Validate readiness with a fresh player action
text: A selection countdown can force a session to start, but it cannot prove that every player is present and tracked; the source's 50-second timer could force readiness without validating players. Require a fresh, attributable action such as a step, press or hold before marking each player ready, and keep that one-time readiness signal separate from continuous movement input. Revalidate a player after hardware loss instead of treating an old position or held input as consent to continue.
use_when: Onboarding several tracked players before a timed or competitive session
do: Confirm each player with a new deliberate action
Separate readiness events from movement targets
Recheck readiness after tracking loss
avoid: Using a timeout alone as proof that players are ready
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Build boss chapters from four waves
text: For a chaptered action game, start with four enemy waves before each boss; tuning converged on four after trying three, four, and five. You can remove pauses between waves for relentless pressure while retaining a separate stage-transition countdown and a pause after the boss dies, giving intensity a clear beginning and end.
use_when: Pacing chapters and bosses in a battle game
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Give respawning players three seconds of grace
text: Start with about 3 seconds of post-respawn protection, rather than 1.5 seconds, so players can reorient before taking damage again. Treat this as a playtest starting point, not a universal value: the doubled timing came from a different death model, so immediate danger, spawn position, and whether the player loses health or is destroyed all affect the right grace period.
use_when: Tuning deaths, respawns, and early-game frustration
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Make shared-station turn order survive walkaways
text: When several visitors share an interactive station, establish priority in join order at each round reset and whenever the active player changes. A visitor who steps away and later returns should rejoin the queue rather than reclaim an old turn; this keeps ownership legible and prevents stale claims from blocking newcomers.
use_when: Designing turn-taking for a public or group installation
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Leave room for tracking lag in walking challenges
text: For position-tracked walking games, tune interactions for delayed and smoothed movement rather than instant input: this setup caps normal UWB motion at 1.8 m/s, predicts at most 0.35 seconds ahead, and treats poses older than 1 second as stale. Use broad checkpoints and hazards, avoid rapid precision dodges, and never depend on movements finer than the 0.08 m position dead zone. Test recovery after tracking errors as well as normal play, since position jumps over 0.75 m may be rejected.
use_when: Setting hazard sizes, movement speed, or dodge timing in a tracked walking game
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Make floor input recover from stuck sensors
text: On pressure-sensitive floors, expect debris, water, a dropped bag, or an overly sensitive sensor to report a press that never ends. Temporarily ignore a cell held longer than any intentional player stance, then restore it automatically after it goes quiet; provide a test view that distinguishes active and muted cells. Set the hold timeout well above the longest deliberate stand, and the gap tolerance above the controller repeat interval of roughly 10–170 ms, so normal packet gaps do not reset the hold.
use_when: Building or playtesting a game that uses a pressure-sensitive floor
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

title: Design foot input for repeats and sensor faults
text: A pressure floor repeats an occupied cell several times per second and provides no release event, so game actions must tolerate repeated messages rather than assume clean press and release pairs. Trigger once per footfall or deliberately accumulate dwell time, preserve each packet's arrival time, and discard stale packets because a delayed frame is indistinguishable from a new step. Temporarily mute cells that stay active longer than a real step, and show muted cells differently from fresh presses so faults are visible without becoming gameplay input.
use_when: Building or playtesting interactions driven by stepping on sensor cells
do: Debounce repeated cell events or intentionally accumulate them into dwell actions
Timestamp arriving steps and reject stale input
Mute abnormally long activations and distinguish them in diagnostics
avoid: Scoring once for every repeated sensor packet
Depending on a hardware release event
Treating a stuck cell as continuous player intent
source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project
